h1: Getting the best from malt extract without dark twangy beer
title: Malt Extract Brewing Without Twang | Craft Beer School
desc: Why extract beers turn out dark and twangy and how to avoid it: fresh extract, late additions, full boils, storage in Indian heat and yeast care.
teaser: Extract brewing does not have to taste like extract. Most of the twang comes from three fixable habits.
standfirst: Malt extract has a bad reputation for dark, caramel-heavy beer with a strange tang. Most of that comes down to old extract, long boils and poor fermentation. Here is how to brew clean, pale beer from a tin or a bag.
sections: Malt extract is wort that a maltster has already mashed, then concentrated. Liquid malt extract (LME) is a thick syrup with about 20% water. Dry malt extract (DME) is spray-dried to a powder. Both let you skip the mash and go straight to the boil, which is why most of us started with them. If you are still deciding which route to take, read extract vs all-grain brewing.

Extract is full of sugars and amino acids. Heat makes them react with each other, the Maillard reaction that browns toast. It happens slowly in the tin on a shelf and quickly in a long boil.

So extract beers darken for two reasons. The extract was already darker from age, or it was boiled for a full hour at high concentration. A tin of pale LME that has sat in a hot warehouse for a year can be noticeably darker than a fresh one. Our guide to beer colour explains how small reactions show up in the glass.

"Extract twang" is a loose description of a slightly sharp, metallic or cooked tang. It is not one compound. The usual causes:

  • Stale extract. LME picks up oxidised, stewed flavours with age and heat.
  • Overloaded minerals. Extract already contains the minerals from the maltster's water. Adding brewing salts on top can make the beer taste harsh.
  • Poor fermentation. Warm, stressed yeast throws off flavours that people blame on the extract.
  • Too much crystal malt. Steeping lots of crystal with extract that already carries caramel character gives a cloying beer.
Buy fresh and store it cool

Most extract in India is imported, which means it may have spent weeks in a container and months in a warm store. Check the date on every tin or bag before you buy. Choose DME if you can. As a dry powder it keeps far better than syrup.

At home, keep extract in the coolest place you have. An opened bag of DME absorbs moisture quickly in humid weather and turns into a solid brick, so seal it tightly and use it within a few weeks. Buy LME close to brew day rather than stockpiling.

A simple test on a tin of LME is to compare it with the colour on the label or a fresh tin in the same shop. If it looks like treacle when the label promises pale, leave it on the shelf.

Always choose the lightest extract that suits the style. You can darken a beer with steeped grains. You cannot lighten one.
Add most of the extract late

This is the single biggest improvement for most extract brewers. Hops need a full boil to give bitterness, but the extract does not need to boil for an hour. It is already sterile and already has its proteins sorted.

  1. Start the boil with roughly a third of your extract to give the hops some sugar to work in.
  2. Run your hop schedule as normal.
  3. Add the remaining extract in the last 10 to 15 minutes, stirring well off the heat so it does not scorch on the base of the pot.

Less time at high temperature means less browning and less cooked flavour. The floor detail worth remembering: LME poured into a pot on a live flame sinks and burns on the bottom within seconds. Turn the flame off, stir it in fully, then relight.
Boil as much volume as you can

Steeping grains are a separate question. A small amount of crystal or specialty malt, steeped at 65 to 70 °C for 30 minutes in a bag before the boil, adds freshness and character that extract alone lacks. Keep crystal modest, roughly 5 to 10% of the fermentables. Leave out roasted malts unless the style needs them.

Many extract recipes tell you to boil 8 to 10 litres and top up with water. A concentrated boil darkens more and uses hops less efficiently. If your pot and stove allow it, boil close to your full batch volume. If you top up, use clean, chlorine-free water. Bottled drinking water or RO water is fine. Borewell water with a strong mineral taste is not.

A lot of what gets blamed on extract is really a fermentation problem. Pitch enough healthy yeast, rehydrate dry yeast properly and keep fermentation temperature steady, ideally 18 to 20 °C for most ales. In Indian summers that means a water bath, a wet towel and a fan, or a fridge with a controller. Our guide on first homebrew mistakes covers the usual traps.

Fresh extract, late additions and a cool, steady fermentation will give you a pale, clean beer that friends would not guess came from a tin. Understanding why each of those steps works (and what to change when a beer still disappoints) is where brewing gets interesting.
faqs: Is dry malt extract better than liquid?
For storage, yes. DME keeps longer and darkens more slowly than LME, which matters when extract has travelled a long way and sat in warm storage.
Can I add all the extract at the end of the boil?
Most brewers add about a third at the start so the hops have some sugar to work in, then the rest in the last 10 to 15 minutes.
Should I add brewing salts to extract beer?
Usually not much. Extract already contains the maltster's minerals, so extra salts can make the beer taste harsh.
